blogs.title: From Cameo to Comment: The Second Circuit’s Objective Turn on Transformative Use
blogs.description: This post unpacks how Santos v. Kimmel applies the Supreme Court’s Warhol framework to late-night satire. The panel rejects Santos’s argument that Kimmel’s fake-name prompts made him the “designer” of the videos’ original purpose, emphasizing instead an objective inquiry into what a reasonable observer would see: Santos’s Cameos conveyed encouragement and positivity, while JKL used them to comment on his willingness to say absurd things for money. The post explains why that purpose difference drives factor one, how the court comfortably resolves fair use at the pleading stage under TCA Television and Cariou, and what this means for media defendants who incorporate user-generated or commissioned content into commentary.

blogs.title: Fair Use Without Good Faith? Deception, Satire, and the Shrinking Role of ‘Bad Faith’
blogs.description: Kimmel obtained the videos under fictitious names, yet the Second Circuit downplays Harper & Row’s ‘good faith’ dictum, aligning with a long-running trend that deception does not defeat fair use when the use is critical or non-substitutive. This piece situates Santos within that trajectory (think NXIVM v. Ross, Swatch, Google Books), showing how the court pivots to market substitution and commentary purpose rather than moral judgments about the user’s conduct. It also flags the limits: deception aimed at usurping a legitimate licensing market could still matter—just not on these facts.

blogs.title: No Third-Party Beneficiary, No Case: Platform ToS and the Limits of Creator Enforcement
blogs.description: Beyond copyright, Santos’s contract theories faltered because he wasn’t a party—or third-party beneficiary—to Cameo’s user Terms (governed by Illinois law), and he failed to plead an implied-in-fact agreement under New York law. This post analyzes the court’s insistence on an almost ‘express declaration’ to confer third-party beneficiary status and the complaint’s failure to allege essential contract terms or a meeting of the minds. It then explores practical takeaways for platforms and creators: drafting ToS to expressly grant creators enforcement rights; structuring direct creator–user terms; and the open question the panel left unresolved—whether such claims would be preempted by the Copyright Act if properly pled.

blogs.title: Markets for Lampoon, Not Licensing: Factor Four (and Three) in the Age of Cameo
blogs.description: Santos argued harm from JKL’s airing of his Cameos, but the Second Circuit doubles down on Hachette’s ‘usurpation versus devaluation’ lens: criticism that may devalue a work isn’t the same as offering a substitute for it. This post explains why late-night ridicule does not compete with the market for personalized shout-outs, and why the court’s note that the videos were ‘published’ undercuts any factor-two appeal. It also discusses the quiet factor-three point—JKL used the whole videos, but that can be justified when the use is commentary-driven—offering guidance to media lawyers on how the amount-taken and market-harm analyses interact in comedic and news segments.
